title: Invert the failure
principles: P07 Vow to become a master

say: Most planning asks how to succeed. Today we turn it upside down and ask how this project will fail.
It sounds pessimistic. In practice it is one of the fastest ways to make something work.

scenes.lead: Imagine it's Doomsday and the demo is dead.
scenes.headline: WHAT *KILLED* IT?
say: Imagine it is Doomsday, week six. You stand up to show your project and it does not work. Something has gone wrong.
What killed it? Answer quickly. Your first three answers are usually the most useful.
The fourth thinking tool is inversion. The question: what would make this fail, and what can I prevent?
Notice the second half. Inversion is never just a list of fears. Every risk ends with an action.

scenes.headline: HOW PROJECTS DIE.

items.d: Broken link, wrong permissions, one device only.
Built for an audience that does not exist.
Scope grew faster than the hours.

say: Three of the most common ways a project dies.
Nobody can open it. A broken link, the wrong permissions, a file that only works on your laptop.
Nobody asked for it. It was built for an audience that turned out not to exist.
Nobody finished it. The scope kept growing faster than the hours available.
Each one is preventable, and each one is cheaper to prevent than to fix.

scenes.kicker: Omar / building a client tool / week 3
say: Omar is building a small tool for his clients. He is excited and wants to add one more feature this week.
He runs inversion first. How would this fail at Doomsday? The answer comes fast. The client cannot open it. He has only ever tested it on his own laptop.

scenes.kicker: Three uses of the same hour

cols.title: Another feature
cols.text: More to show. Same risk of showing nothing.

cols.title: A list of fears
cols.text: Twelve risks. No actions. Anxiety, documented.

cols.title: Prevent the likeliest failure
cols.text: Phone, tablet, a friend's laptop. Two bugs found.

scenes.quote: Risk: client can't open it. Prevention: test on three devices before adding anything.
say: Three ways to spend the hour.
Add the feature. More to show, and exactly the same chance of showing nothing.
Write a list of fears. Twelve risks and no actions. That is anxiety with a spreadsheet. The limit on this tool: risk listing can become avoidance. Always finish with an action.
Prevent the likeliest failure. He tests the tool on his phone, a tablet and a friend's laptop. He finds two bugs that would have ended the demo. Then he adds the feature.

scenes.question: What one _skill_ would make _this_ *better?*
scenes.sub: Pick something small enough to practise twice this week, with feedback.
say: This week you also choose one subskill to practise with feedback. Inversion helps here too. Which weakness is most likely to hurt the project?

Choose something small enough to practise twice this week. Writing a clearer headline. Explaining your offer in thirty seconds. Testing on a second device. Principle seven, vow to become a master, starts with deliberate practice on one small thing.

scenes.headline: RUN YOUR PRE-MORTEM.
items: Imagine the Doomsday demo has failed.
Write the three most likely causes.
Schedule the first action this week.
say: Pause the video when I tell you to.
One. Imagine the Doomsday demo has failed.
Two. Write the three most likely causes.
Three. Give each one a preventive action.
Four. Put the first action in your calendar this week. Pause now and give it five minutes.

rows: One action for each of three risks.
say: Your mission is workbook page W03-D02, design against failure.
Complete your three-risk prevention sheet and take the first preventive action today if you can.

scenes.next: Next / Lesson 09 / Build your first Doombot
say: Next lesson you build your first Doombot: a small, reusable aid that takes repetition off your hands.
Know how it dies. Then don't let it. Prevention is the cheapest fix you will ever make.
